The workarounds are setter injection, which lets Spring create both objects first and wire them afterwards, and @Lazy on one side, which injects a proxy that resolves the real bean on first use. Spring Boot 2.6 and later disables circular references by default, so relying on the setter workaround now requires explicitly allowing it, which is another reason to fix the design instead.
followUps: Why does constructor injection make cycles fail fast instead of hiding them?
How does @Lazy break the cycle?
question: What is a circular dependency in Spring, and how do you fix one?
shortAnswer: A circular dependency is when bean A needs B and B needs A, so neither can be constructed first. Spring detects it at startup; the real fix is to redesign, for example by extracting a shared component, and the workarounds are setter injection or @Lazy.
tips: Say the failure is useful: it exposes a design problem.
Give the redesign first, the workarounds second.
title: Circular dependencies in Spring

commonMistakes: Claiming @Service adds transaction or caching behaviour.
Annotating everything @Component and losing the layering.
detailedAnswer: Technically @Service and @Repository are meta-annotated with @Component, so all three make a class a Spring bean discovered by component scanning. The difference is meaning and one behaviour. @Component is the generic marker for any Spring-managed class. @Service marks the service layer, which tells readers where business logic lives and gives pointcuts and tooling something to key on. @Repository marks the persistence layer and adds exception translation: a JPA or JDBC exception is converted into a Spring DataAccessException, so callers deal with one consistent exception hierarchy instead of vendor-specific ones. @Controller and @RestController follow the same pattern for the web layer. Because the difference is mostly semantic, the value is in consistency: if a class is a service, annotate it @Service, so the architecture is visible in the code.
followUps: Which of the three changes runtime behaviour, and how?
Where does @Controller fit in this family?
question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?
shortAnswer: All three register a bean, and @Service and @Repository are specialisations of @Component that document intent; @Repository additionally translates persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy, while @Service carries no extra behaviour.
tips: State plainly that only @Repository adds behaviour.
Mention exception translation as the one real difference.
title: @Component versus @Service versus @Repository

commonMistakes: Doing heavy work in a runner and delaying application readiness.
Parsing raw args by hand when ApplicationRunner does it for you.
detailedAnswer: Use a runner for startup work such as seeding data, warming a cache, or validating configuration. CommandLineRunner is the simpler one: run(String... args) hands you the raw command-line strings, and you parse them yourself. ApplicationRunner is the friendlier one: run(ApplicationArguments args) gives you getOptionNames(), getOptionValues("port"), and getNonOptionArgs(), so --port=9090 is already parsed for you. If you define several runners, control their order with @Order, because the order is otherwise unspecified. Two cautions: a runner that throws will stop the application from starting, which is useful for fail-fast validation but bad for optional work, and long-running startup tasks delay readiness, so heavy work usually belongs in a background thread or a scheduled job instead.
followUps: How do you control the order of multiple runners?
What happens if a runner throws an exception?
question: What is the difference between CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner in Spring Boot?
shortAnswer: Both run code after the application context is ready but before the application is considered started; CommandLineRunner receives the raw String[] arguments, while ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments with named options and non-option arguments separated.
tips: Show the --port=9090 example for ApplicationRunner.
Warn that a failing runner stops startup.
title: CommandLineRunner versus ApplicationRunner

commonMistakes: Assuming @Value accepts relaxed names.
A typo in a property name silently binding to nothing.
detailedAnswer: Spring Boot does not require the property name to match the Java field exactly. For a field named maxSize, all of these bind: app.max-size, app.max_size, app.maxSize, and the environment variable APP_MAX_SIZE. That is why the same application can be configured from a properties file, a YAML file, and environment variables without renaming anything. The binding is done by @ConfigurationProperties on a class, which is the recommended approach because it gives you a typed, validated object instead of scattered @Value annotations. Two things to remember: relaxed binding does not apply to @Value, which requires an exact match, and a typo that is still a valid relaxed form will silently bind to nothing, so enable strict validation or check the bound values at startup.
followUps: Does relaxed binding work with @Value?
How do you validate a @ConfigurationProperties class at startup?
question: What is relaxed binding, and how does it work with @ConfigurationProperties?
shortAnswer: Relaxed binding lets a property be written in several forms, such as app.max-size, app.maxSize, or APP_MAX_SIZE, and still bind to the same Java field; it applies to @ConfigurationProperties and to @Value only in limited cases.
tips: Give the four spellings of one property as the example.
Recommend @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value.
title: Relaxed binding in Spring Boot configuration

commonMistakes: Leaving the Whitelabel page in front of API clients.
Exposing stack traces in production error responses.
detailedAnswer: When a request fails and no handler covers it, Spring Boot renders a plain error page that shows the status, the error, and a timestamp. That is acceptable for a browser demo but wrong for an API, where clients need a machine-readable JSON body with a stable shape: a code, a message, and ideally a correlation id. The standard fix is a @ControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods that build a ResponseEntity with the right status and body, for example 404 for a missing resource and 400 for a validation failure. For browser-facing applications, placing an error/404.html or error/500.html template under src/main/resources/templates replaces the Whitelabel page for those statuses. You can also set server.error.include-message and include-stacktrace to control how much detail leaks into responses, and in production they should stay minimal.
followUps: How do you return a consistent JSON error body for all failures?
What should server.error.include-stacktrace be in production, and why?
question: What is the Whitelabel error page, and how do you replace it with a proper error response?
shortAnswer: The Whitelabel page is Spring Boot's default HTML error page for unhandled errors; for APIs you replace it with a @ControllerAdvice that returns a consistent JSON error body, or with a custom error.html template for browser pages.
tips: Contrast the browser case (template) with the API case (@ControllerAdvice).
Mention the stack-trace setting as a security point.
title: The Whitelabel error page and custom error handling

commonMistakes: Forgetting SpringBootServletInitializer, so the WAR deploys but never starts.
Shipping the embedded Tomcat inside a WAR and getting class clashes.
detailedAnswer: The executable JAR is the default and the recommended path: java -jar app.jar starts the embedded server, and the deployment is one artifact with one process. A WAR is for environments where an external Tomcat or Jetty is mandated, for example an operations team that manages a shared container. The changes are threefold: packaging war in the build file, the spring-boot-starter-tomcat dependency marked as provided so it does not clash with the container's own Tomcat, and the main class extending SpringBootServletInitializer and overriding configure() to point at the application class. The WAR then loses the embedded server's simplicity: you cannot just run it, and the container's version and configuration become part of your deployment. Unless policy forces it, keep the JAR.
followUps: What does SpringBootServletInitializer do?
Why must the embedded Tomcat be marked provided in a WAR build?
question: How do you deploy a Spring Boot application as a WAR instead of an executable JAR, and why would you?
shortAnswer: By default Spring Boot builds an executable JAR with an embedded server; to produce a WAR you change the packaging, mark the embedded Tomcat as provided, and extend SpringBootServletInitializer so the external container can bootstrap the app. You only do this when an existing servlet container or ops policy requires it.
tips: List the three concrete changes.
State the recommendation plainly: JAR unless policy forces WAR.
title: Deploying Spring Boot as a JAR versus a WAR

commonMistakes: Disabling CSRF because a form broke, instead of adding the token.
Assuming a JWT in a cookie is safe from CSRF.
detailedAnswer: The attack works because browsers attach cookies automatically: a malicious page can make the victim's browser submit a form to your bank's transfer endpoint, and the session cookie goes along, so the server cannot tell the request came from the attacker. Spring Security defends this by requiring a CSRF token, a secret value rendered into your forms and checked on every state-changing request, so a request from another origin fails the check. Disabling it is safe only when the application does not rely on cookies for authentication at all, for example a stateless API using an Authorization bearer token, because then the browser has no ambient credential to abuse. For a traditional server-rendered app with session cookies, disabling CSRF leaves the application open, and the fix for a broken form is usually to include the token, not to turn the protection off.
followUps: Why does a bearer-token API not need CSRF protection?
How does the CSRF token actually stop the attack?
question: What is CSRF, and when is it safe to disable CSRF protection in Spring Boot?
shortAnswer: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to your site, using the browser's stored session cookie. Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default; it is safe to disable only for stateless APIs, such as JWT bearer-token APIs, where no cookie authenticates the request.
tips: Explain the attack in one sentence before the defence.
Give the rule: disable only when no cookie authenticates requests.
title: CSRF protection in Spring Security

commonMistakes: Catching everything in each controller with try-catch.
Throwing generic RuntimeException, which the advice cannot distinguish.
detailedAnswer: Without central handling, every controller repeats try-catch blocks and errors come back in different shapes. A @ControllerAdvice class is a global version of a controller: methods annotated with @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) run whenever that exception escapes any controller, and they return a ResponseEntity with a status and a uniform body, for example a code, a message, and a timestamp. You can also extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler to override handling for Spring's own exceptions, such as validation failures, so they use the same error shape. The exceptions themselves should stay meaningful: throw a specific ResourceNotFoundException from the service layer instead of a generic RuntimeException, because the advice can only map what it can distinguish.
followUps: How do you make validation errors use the same error shape?
Where should the exception be thrown: controller or service?
question: How do you handle exceptions globally in a Spring MVC application?
shortAnswer: Use a @ControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods: each method maps an exception type to a ResponseEntity with the right status and a consistent error body, so no controller needs its own try-catch.
tips: Stress the consistency win: one error shape for the whole API.
Mention ResponseEntityExceptionHandler for Spring's own exceptions.
title: Global exception handling with @ControllerAdvice

commonMistakes: Trusting the file extension for validation.
Storing uploads in a web-accessible directory.
detailedAnswer: Spring Boot configures a MultipartResolver automatically, so a controller method can declare @RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file and receive the upload. The checks that matter are server-side: reject empty files, enforce a size limit, and validate the content type by inspecting the bytes rather than trusting the extension, because the extension is whatever the client claims. Store the file with a generated name in a directory outside the web root, or in object storage such as S3, and keep only the path in the database. Never save a file under its original filename in a web-accessible folder: a crafted name can overwrite other files or, if the file is executable, lead to remote code execution. The size limits live in configuration, and exceeding them produces a MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which your @ControllerAdvice should turn into a clean 413 or 400 response.
followUps: Why should you never store an upload under its original filename?
What happens when an upload exceeds the configured size limit?
question: How do you handle a file upload in a Spring MVC controller?
shortAnswer: Accept a MultipartFile with @RequestParam, validate its size and type, and store it on disk or in object storage; configure limits with spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size, and never trust the client-supplied filename.
tips: Lead with the security point: never trust the filename.
Mention the size-limit exception and its handler.
title: Handling file uploads in Spring MVC

commonMistakes: Joining a table to itself without aliases.
Using an inner join and dropping employees without a manager.
detailedAnswer: A self-join is an ordinary join where both sides are the same table, distinguished by aliases: FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id. Without the aliases the query is ambiguous and the database cannot tell which copy of the table a column belongs to. The manager example is the standard one: to list each employee with their manager's name, you join the table to itself on the manager id, and a LEFT JOIN keeps employees with no manager instead of dropping them. Other uses are comparing rows, such as finding pairs of employees in the same department, and hierarchical data before recursive queries exist. The key point for the interview is that there is nothing special about the syntax: it is a normal join, and the aliases are what make it work.
followUps: How would you list employees who have no manager?
How would you find pairs of employees in the same department?
question: What is a self-join, and when would you use one?
shortAnswer: A self-join joins a table to itself using two aliases, so you can compare rows within the same table; the classic case is an employees table where each employee references a manager who is also an employee.
tips: Use the employee-manager example; it is the canonical one.
Point out that aliases are the whole trick.
title: Self-join in SQL

commonMistakes: Writing a correlated subquery that runs once per row.
Using NOT IN with nulls, which silently returns no rows.
detailedAnswer: A join is the natural tool for combining related rows: orders with their customer names, employees with their departments. A subquery is the natural tool for a question that is itself a query: employees whose salary is above the average, orders from customers who have ordered more than five times, or an EXISTS check, which stops at the first match and is often the fastest way to test existence. Correlated subqueries, which run once per outer row, are the performance trap: they look innocent and scale terribly, and rewriting one as a join is a standard optimisation. As a rule, prefer joins for combining, prefer subqueries for filtering by an aggregate or an existence test, and always check with EXPLAIN rather than guessing, because the optimiser often rewrites one form into the other anyway.
followUps: Why is a correlated subquery usually slower than a join?
When is EXISTS faster than IN?
question: When would you use a JOIN, and when is a subquery the better choice?
shortAnswer: Use a JOIN when you need columns from both tables or when the relationship is the point of the query; use a subquery when you need a single value, an existence check, or a filtered set first. JOINs are usually faster, but readability decides when performance is equal.
tips: Give the rule: join to combine, subquery to filter by a computed value.
Mention EXPLAIN as the arbiter.
title: JOIN versus subquery: how to choose

commonMistakes: Using @Modifying without @Transactional.
Reading stale entities after a bulk update without clearing the context.
detailedAnswer: Derived query methods and @Query methods are reads by default; Spring Data JPA will reject an update query unless the method is annotated with @Modifying. The annotation tells Spring to call executeUpdate instead of getResultList and to return the number of affected rows. Two things are commonly forgotten. First, the transaction: a modifying query needs an active transaction, so the method needs @Transactional, or it fails at runtime. Second, staleness: entities already loaded in the persistence context are not refreshed by a bulk update, so a later read can return old values; setting clearAutomatically = true clears the context after the update, and flushAutomatically = true flushes pending changes before it. For large bulk operations, a bulk update is far cheaper than loading every entity and saving it one by one.
followUps: What goes wrong if you forget @Transactional on a @Modifying method?
Why might a read after a bulk update return stale data?
question: What is @Modifying for in Spring Data JPA, and what do people forget when they use it?
shortAnswer: @Modifying marks a @Query as a write: an UPDATE or DELETE instead of a SELECT. It must run inside a transaction, so the method also needs @Transactional, and the persistence context can hold stale entities unless you clear it with clearAutomatically.
tips: Name the two forgotten pieces: the transaction and the stale context.
Mention the bulk-update cost saving.
title: @Modifying in Spring Data JPA

commonMistakes: Forgetting equals and hashCode on the key class.
Using a composite key when a surrogate id would be simpler.
detailedAnswer: Some tables are naturally identified by two columns, such as an order line identified by order id plus line number. JPA offers two mappings. With @EmbeddedId, you write one small class annotated @Embeddable that holds both fields, and the entity has a single @EmbeddedId field of that type; the key is one object, which is easy to pass around and use in queries. With @IdClass, the entity declares both key fields directly with @Id, and the id class mirrors them; this keeps the entity's fields flat but duplicates the field definitions. Whichever you choose, the key class must implement equals and hashCode correctly and be Serializable, because JPA and collections both depend on them. A practical tip: if the table has no natural composite key and you control the schema, a single surrogate id is usually simpler than a composite key.
followUps: What must a composite key class implement, and why?
When would you avoid a composite key entirely?
question: How do you map an entity whose primary key is made of two columns?
shortAnswer: Use a composite key: either an @Embeddable key class held in one @EmbeddedId field, or an @IdClass that mirrors the key fields on the entity. @EmbeddedId is the cleaner and more common choice.
tips: Recommend @EmbeddedId and say why.
Mention the surrogate-key escape hatch.
title: Composite keys in JPA: @EmbeddedId versus @IdClass

commonMistakes: Applying eventual consistency to money movement.
Assuming a read immediately after a write sees the new value.
detailedAnswer: Strong consistency, the kind a single database gives you with ACID transactions, is impossible across independent services without expensive coordination, so distributed systems trade it for availability and partition tolerance. With eventual consistency, a write to one service propagates to the others through events, and readers may briefly see the old value. Whether that is fine is a business question, not a technical one: a like count that is off by one for a second is harmless, but a bank balance that is off by one is not. The design consequences are concrete: clients must tolerate stale reads, often with read-your-writes guarantees for the user who just wrote, operations must be idempotent because events can be delivered twice, and the UI should be designed so a brief inconsistency is invisible rather than alarming.
followUps: How do you give a user a read-your-writes guarantee with eventual consistency?
Why must event handlers be idempotent?
question: What is eventual consistency, and when is it acceptable?
shortAnswer: Eventual consistency means replicas and services may disagree briefly after a write, but converge to the same value if no new writes arrive. It is acceptable when the business can tolerate a short delay, such as counts and feeds, and unacceptable when money moves, such as balances and inventory reservations.
tips: Frame it as a business decision with examples on both sides.
Mention idempotency as the practical consequence.
title: Eventual consistency in microservices

commonMistakes: Assuming a registry outage stops all traffic.
Treating a cached registry entry as permanently valid.
detailedAnswer: The registry, such as Eureka or Consul, is the phone book: services register on startup and clients look up addresses before calling. If it fails, the damage is limited by design. Clients cache the registry entries they have already fetched, so calls between already-known services continue, and Eureka's self-preservation mode deliberately stops evicting instances during a network problem rather than dropping healthy services. What breaks is change: new instances cannot be found, dead instances keep being tried until the cache refreshes, and deployments that depend on discovery stall. That is why the registry itself runs as a cluster, why clients must handle a stale entry with retries and timeouts, and why critical paths often add a fallback such as a static list or a load balancer in front of the registry.
followUps: Why do clients cache the registry, and what risk does the cache carry?
What is Eureka's self-preservation mode?
question: What happens in a microservices system if the service registry goes down?
shortAnswer: New services cannot register and new instances cannot be discovered, but existing services keep working because clients cache the registry locally; the registry is therefore designed for high availability, and clients fall back to their cached copy.
tips: Lead with the reassuring fact: existing traffic keeps flowing.
Name the real casualty: change and discovery of new instances.
title: What happens when the service registry fails?

commonMistakes: Forgetting that -15 starts with a minus sign.
Writing a manual loop when the question asks for streams.
followUps: How would you do it without converting to strings?
How do negative numbers change the answer?
question: Given a list of integers, find all numbers starting with 1 using Stream functions. What is your approach?
shortAnswer: Convert each number to its string form, keep the ones whose first character is 1, and collect the result; the conversion is the trick, because streams have no numeric 'starts with' operation.
tips: Say why the string conversion is the trick, not the filter.
Mention the negative-number edge case.
title: Coding: numbers starting with 1 using streams

commonMistakes: Saying JDK proxies work for any class.
Forgetting that final methods escape CGLIB proxies.
detailedAnswer: A JDK dynamic proxy is a runtime-generated class that implements the same interfaces as the target, so it only works when the bean implements an interface and only intercepts interface methods. A CGLIB proxy is a runtime-generated subclass of the target class, so it works with no interface, but a subclass cannot override a final method or extend a final class, so those are never advised. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies, which is why injecting a bean by its concrete class usually works even when the bean implements an interface.
followUps: What happens if you inject a JDK-proxied bean by its concrete class?
Why can't a CGLIB proxy advise a final method?
question: How does Spring decide between a JDK dynamic proxy and a CGLIB proxy, and what can each one not do?
shortAnswer: A JDK proxy implements the bean's interfaces and needs one; a CGLIB proxy subclasses the bean and works without an interface, but cannot proxy final classes or methods. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default.
tips: Name the default first: Spring Boot uses CGLIB unless configured otherwise.
Tie the answer to a failure: a final method silently skipping advice is the classic symptom.
title: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB

commonMistakes: Claiming Spring will warn you — it does not.
Suggesting @Transactional on the calling method as a fix when the point is the called method's own boundary.
detailedAnswer: The @Transactional behaviour is an interceptor on the proxy that wraps the bean. Calls arriving from outside go through the proxy and start a transaction; a method calling another method on the same object calls this directly, bypassing the proxy entirely. The annotation is silently ignored — no error, no warning. The same applies to @Async, @Cacheable, and @PreAuthorize. Fixes: have another bean call the annotated method, inject the bean into itself through the proxy, or restructure so the caller invokes the transactional method directly.
followUps: Does @Transactional work on a private method?
How would you fix it without restructuring the classes?
question: A service method calls another @Transactional method in the same class, and no transaction starts. Why?
shortAnswer: Spring applies transactions through a proxy, and a call on this never passes through the proxy, so the transactional advice never runs.
tips: Draw the proxy in words: outside call goes through it, internal call does not.
Mention that the same trap applies to @Async and @Cacheable — interviewers love the generalisation.
title: Why @Transactional fails on self-invocation

commonMistakes: Saying mappedBy owns the relationship.
Claiming both sides are written to the database.
detailedAnswer: In a bidirectional association only one side owns the foreign key. For an order and its line items, the @ManyToOne side (LineItem.order, with @JoinColumn) owns it, and the @OneToMany side declares mappedBy = "order" to say so. Hibernate writes only the owning side's state: adding a child to the parent's collection without setting child.setOrder(parent) inserts the child with a null foreign key. The standard fix is a helper method on the parent that sets both sides, so the in-memory graph and the database row cannot disagree.
followUps: What happens if you set only the inverse side?
When would you model a many-to-many with an explicit link entity?
question: What does mappedBy mean on a @OneToMany, and which side of the association owns the relationship?
shortAnswer: mappedBy marks the inverse side. The owning side — usually the @ManyToOne — holds the foreign key and is the only side Hibernate writes.
tips: Answer with the foreign key: whoever holds it owns the relationship.
Mention the helper-method pattern — it shows you have debugged this.
title: mappedBy and association ownership

commonMistakes: Treating the two as the same feature.
Enabling orphanRemoval on a shared association.
detailedAnswer: Cascade propagates an operation you perform: with CascadeType.REMOVE, calling remove() on the parent deletes the children too. orphanRemoval is different — it reacts to the state of the collection: removing a child from the parent's list deletes that child's row at flush time, with no explicit delete call. orphanRemoval is the right tool for privately owned children such as order line items, and the wrong tool for shared entities, where removing a reference from one parent should not delete a row other parents still use.
followUps: Would you cascade REMOVE from a parent to a shared entity?
What does CascadeType.PERSIST do?
question: What is the difference between CascadeType.REMOVE and orphanRemoval on a @OneToMany?
shortAnswer: Cascade REMOVE deletes children when you explicitly delete the parent; orphanRemoval deletes a child when it is removed from the parent's collection, even though the parent still exists.
tips: Contrast the trigger: an explicit operation versus a missing reference.
Give the line-item example for orphanRemoval.
title: Cascade REMOVE vs orphanRemoval

commonMistakes: Saying ReentrantLock is faster — it is not, it is more flexible.
Forgetting unlock() on the exception path.
detailedAnswer: synchronized is the default: simple, automatically released, and understood by the JVM. ReentrantLock adds tryLock() (attempt without blocking), tryLock(timeout, unit) (give up after a wait instead of blocking forever), lockInterruptibly() (let a waiting thread be cancelled), an optional fairness policy, and multiple Condition objects per lock (for example separate not-full and not-empty conditions in a bounded buffer). The price is explicit release: every lock() must be paired with unlock() in a finally block, or an exception leaves the lock held forever.
followUps: What does a Condition give you that wait/notify does not?
Why is fairness usually left off?
question: When would you choose ReentrantLock over synchronized?
shortAnswer: When you need a timeout, an interruptible wait, fairness, or multiple Conditions — none of which synchronized offers.
tips: List the four features, then name the cost: manual unlock in finally.
Give the bounded-buffer example for multiple Conditions.
title: ReentrantLock vs synchronized

commonMistakes: Saying virtual threads are faster — they make blocking cheap, not computation fast.
Forgetting that synchronized is the pinning cause.
detailedAnswer: A platform thread maps one-to-one to an operating system thread and occupies it while blocked. A virtual thread runs on a carrier thread from a small pool; when it blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it and the carrier runs another virtual thread, so a million virtual threads can be alive at once. Pinning breaks that: blocking while holding a monitor (synchronized) or inside a native call keeps the virtual thread mounted, so the carrier cannot do other work and the pool can starve under load. The fix is to use ReentrantLock, which does not pin, and to keep blocking calls out of synchronized blocks.
followUps: Why should you not pool virtual threads?
Does a virtual thread help CPU-bound work?
question: How does a virtual thread differ from a platform thread, and what is pinning?
shortAnswer: A virtual thread is JVM-managed and cheap to block: it unmounts from its carrier platform thread while waiting. Pinning is when it cannot unmount — blocking inside synchronized or a native call — so the carrier stays occupied.
tips: Explain mount and unmount before naming pinning.
Give the ReentrantLock remedy, not just the problem.
title: Virtual threads, carriers, and pinning

commonMistakes: Claiming virtual threads make everything faster.
Creating unbounded virtual threads against a 20-connection pool.
detailedAnswer: Virtual threads help when threads block on I/O: the cost they remove is the cost of a blocked thread. A computation that never blocks gains nothing and pays scheduling overhead, so CPU-bound work belongs on a bounded platform-thread pool. A small, fixed number of tasks is simpler on a platform pool too. And a million concurrent requests still hit one database: without a limit such as a semaphore or a bounded connection pool, virtual threads can overwhelm a downstream service faster than a bounded pool would. They also multiply ThreadLocal state — a million virtual threads can mean a million copies of a ThreadLocal value.
followUps: What executor would you use for virtual threads?
How do you bound concurrency to a database with virtual threads?
question: When should you not use virtual threads?
shortAnswer: For CPU-bound work, for a small fixed set of long-lived tasks, or when the downstream system cannot handle unbounded concurrency — virtual threads remove the thread bottleneck, not the resource bottleneck.
tips: Name the bottleneck virtual threads do not remove.
Mention ThreadLocal as the less obvious hazard.
title: When not to use virtual threads

commonMistakes: Saying the index is hash % capacity.
Saying spreading is done to make hashes random.
detailedAnswer: A key's bucket index is (n - 1) & hash, where n is the table length. Because capacity is always a power of two, n - 1 is a run of 1-bits, so this is equivalent to hash % n but costs a bitwise AND instead of a division. The catch is that only the low bits of the hash decide the bucket — so HashMap first spreads the hash by XOR-ing it with its own top 16 bits, mixing the high bits into the low ones. Without spreading, keys whose hash codes differ only in the high bits would all collide in the same bucket.
followUps: Why must capacity stay a power of two?
What is the default load factor, and when does the table resize?
question: Why does HashMap spread the hash code, and how is the bucket index computed?
shortAnswer: The index uses only the low bits of the hash, so spreading XORs the high bits down ((h ^ (h >>> 16))). The index is (n - 1) & hash, which works because capacity is always a power of two.
tips: Write the two formulas: the spread and (n - 1) & hash.
Explain why the power-of-two capacity matters for the AND trick.
title: HashMap hash spreading and indexing

commonMistakes: Saying ConcurrentHashMap locks the whole map.
Storing null and expecting it to work like HashMap.
detailedAnswer: In concurrent code, map.get(key) returning null must mean one thing: the key is absent. If null values were allowed, a null result could mean absent or present-with-null, and no atomic check could distinguish them. For safety, ConcurrentHashMap inserts into an empty bin with a compare-and-swap (no lock), synchronizes on the first node of an occupied bin so only writers to that bucket contend, lets multiple threads cooperate on a resize, and counts size with counter cells instead of one contended counter. Iterators are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException and may or may not show concurrent updates.
followUps: How would you atomically increment a counter in a ConcurrentHashMap?
When would you still use Collections.synchronizedMap?
question: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values, and how does it stay thread-safe without one big lock?
shortAnswer: Null is forbidden so that get() returning null unambiguously means absent. Safety comes from CAS on empty bins and synchronizing on the first node of an occupied bin — reads never block.
tips: Answer the null question first — it is about ambiguity, not convenience.
Contrast bin-level locking with the old whole-map lock.
title: ConcurrentHashMap nulls and locking

commonMistakes: Describing the implicit flow as the current standard.
Confusing the code with the token.
detailedAnswer: The client redirects the user to the authorization server with the requested scopes and a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier). The user authenticates and consents, and the server redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The client exchanges the code for tokens, sending the original code_verifier; the server checks it against the challenge. Even if the code leaks from the redirect, nobody else can redeem it, because they do not have the verifier. PKCE is required for public clients such as mobile and single-page apps, which cannot keep a secret, and recommended for every client. The older implicit flow, which returned tokens in the redirect itself, is deprecated.
followUps: What is the difference between an access token and an id_token?
Why is the implicit flow deprecated?
question: Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE. What does the code verifier prove?
shortAnswer: The client creates a random verifier, sends its hash as the challenge, and presents the verifier when exchanging the code for tokens — proving the exchange comes from the client that started the flow.
tips: Walk the four steps in order: challenge, consent, code, exchange.
Say what the verifier proves — same client, not just any client.
title: Authorization code flow with PKCE

commonMistakes: Saying primitives always live on the stack.
Saying objects always live on the heap with no exception.
detailedAnswer: The stack holds method frames: local variables (primitive locals and reference variables) and return addresses, freed when the method returns. Objects live on the heap — including their fields, so an int field of an object lives on the heap inside that object, and an int array's elements live on the heap in the array. The JIT compiler can also invert the rule through escape analysis: an object that never escapes its method may be allocated on the stack instead of the heap. The right mental model is about lifetimes, not types: stack data dies with the method call, heap data lives until unreachable.
followUps: Where does a local reference variable live, and where does its object live?
What is escape analysis?
question: Do primitives always live on the stack?
shortAnswer: No. Primitive locals live in stack frames, but primitive fields live on the heap as part of their object — and escape analysis can stack-allocate objects too.
tips: Answer with locals versus fields, not with primitives versus objects.
Mention escape analysis as the exception that proves the rule.
title: Do primitives always live on the stack?

commonMistakes: Saying the two cost the same.
Assuming PostgreSQL tables are clustered like InnoDB's.
detailedAnswer: A clustered index decides the physical order of the table's rows — the table itself is stored in index order, and a table has at most one, usually its primary key (InnoDB stores tables clustered by primary key). A non-clustered (secondary) index maps indexed values to row locations in a separate structure, and the database follows the pointer to fetch the row. A range scan on the clustered key is cheap because the rows are adjacent; a lookup through a secondary index costs a pointer chase per row, and a secondary index returning a large fraction of the table can be slower than a full scan, because random fetches cost more than a sequential read.
followUps: What is a covering index, and why does it avoid the extra hop?
Why can a table have only one clustered index?
question: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
shortAnswer: A clustered index stores the table's rows in index order (one per table, usually the primary key); a non-clustered index is a separate structure that points at rows, so each lookup costs an extra hop.
tips: Lead with physical order versus pointer.
Mention InnoDB's primary-key clustering as the concrete case.
title: Clustered vs non-clustered indexes

commonMistakes: Retrying a poison message forever with no dead-letter topic.
Assuming the dead-letter topic is monitored just because it exists.
Committing offsets before processing so failures vanish silently.
detailedAnswer: A @KafkaListener that throws has its record redelivered, because offsets are committed only after successful processing. Without a failure policy, a poison message — one that fails on every attempt — is retried forever and blocks its whole partition. The standard shape is a DefaultErrorHandler (the current name in Spring Kafka 3.x) with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and a FixedBackOff: after the configured retries, the recoverer publishes the failed record to a dead-letter topic, by default the original topic name plus -dlt, preserving the original headers including the exception, and the container commits the offset. The dead-letter topic must be watched — an alert or dashboard — or it becomes a quieter form of data loss. The listener itself must still be idempotent, because retries before the dead-letter step can run the same record twice.
followUps: Where do dead-lettered records go, and how would you replay one?
Why must the listener still be idempotent even with a dead-letter topic?
question: How do you stop one failing Kafka record from blocking its partition in Spring Boot?
shortAnswer: Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer on the listener container factory: retry the record with a backoff, then publish it to a dead-letter topic and commit the offset so the consumer moves on.
tips: Name the two classes: DefaultErrorHandler and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer.
Mention that the DLT needs monitoring, not just existence.
title: Kafka listeners: retries and dead-letter topics

commonMistakes: Using condition where unless is needed, and wondering why #result is unavailable.
Caching nulls for missing rows with no TTL.
Assuming sync=true works across multiple caches.
detailedAnswer: condition and unless both take SpEL, but at opposite moments. condition runs before the method, so it decides whether caching applies at all — condition = "#id > 0" skips the cache entirely for invalid ids — and it cannot see #result because the method has not run. unless runs after the method, so it judges the computed value — unless = "#result == null" keeps a missing row out of the cache, so a record created later is found immediately instead of serving a cached null until TTL expires. sync=true addresses the stampede: when a hot key expires, concurrent misses for that key block on the first caller, which loads once and shares the value. It works for a single cache only, and it relies on the cache implementation supporting the blocking load, which Spring Data Redis's RedisCache does.
followUps: Why would you cache a null for a missing row at all, and with what TTL?
What happens if you put sync=true on an annotation with several caches?
question: What is the difference between condition and unless on @Cacheable, and what does sync=true do?
shortAnswer: condition is evaluated before the method runs and can only use the arguments; unless is evaluated after and can also use #result. sync=true makes concurrent misses for the same key wait on the first loader instead of all hitting the database.
tips: Anchor on the evaluation moment: condition before, unless after.
Mention that unless is the only one that can see #result.
title: Spring Cache: condition vs unless, and sync=true

commonMistakes: Returning a ProblemDetail and expecting Spring to fill in instance automatically — a custom handler must set it.
Inventing a custom error envelope when the standard exists.
Enabling the property and assuming business exceptions are covered too.
detailedAnswer: RFC 9457 defines one standard JSON shape for API errors instead of every team inventing its own envelope: type (a URI for the problem kind, default about:blank), title (a short summary, same for every occurrence), status, detail (this occurrence, for humans), and instance (this occurrence's URI, usually the request path), plus extension members such as a stable error code added with setProperty. Spring's ProblemDetail models it, and returning one from an @ExceptionHandler sets the response status from its status field and the content type to application/problem+json. For Spring MVC's own exceptions — 404 for an unknown URL, 405, 415 — spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true makes Boot return them in the same shape; it is off by default because it changes every default error body. The fuller version is an advice extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, whose methods already return ProblemDetail for each framework exception. ProblemDetail standardizes the body; @RestControllerAdvice still decides which exception maps to which problem.
followUps: What does spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true change, and why is it off by default?
How do you keep a stable machine-readable error code inside a ProblemDetail?
question: What is ProblemDetail, and how does it relate to RFC 9457?
shortAnswer: ProblemDetail is Spring Framework 6's implementation of RFC 9457 (which supersedes RFC 7807): a standard error body with type, title, status, detail, and instance, served as application/problem+json. Returning one from an @ExceptionHandler sets the status and content type from the object.
tips: Name the five members and the media type.
Note that RFC 9457 supersedes RFC 7807 — interviewers check for the current number.
title: ProblemDetail and RFC 9457 error responses

commonMistakes: Implementing Cloneable and forgetting to deep-copy mutable fields.
Assuming clone() runs a constructor.
Overriding finalize() to clean up instead of using close() and Cleaner.
detailedAnswer: Object.clone() copies field by field: primitives by value, references by reference. That is a shallow copy — the clone and the original share every mutable object they point to, so mutating a list through one mutates it for the other. A deep copy duplicates the mutable parts as well, so the two are independent. clone() is awkward to use correctly: the class must implement Cloneable, a marker interface that declares no clone() method, or clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime even though the code compiled; the override must be public, call super.clone(), and then deep-copy each mutable field by hand; and clone() bypasses constructors, so constructor invariants are not checked on a clone. Cloning an array is shallow too. A copy constructor — new Team(other) — avoids all of it: no interface, no checked exception, the normal constructor path runs, and it works with final fields. That is why Effective Java calls Cloneable broken and prefers copy constructors.
followUps: If a class holds a mutable list, what does a correct clone() have to do?
Why does cloning an array not give you a deep copy?
question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy, and why is clone() risky?
shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the fields, so mutable referenced objects are shared; a deep copy duplicates the mutable parts too. clone() is shallow by default, needs the marker interface Cloneable, bypasses constructors, and throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime — a copy constructor is usually the safer choice.
tips: Trace a concrete example: two objects sharing one list.
Quote the Effective Java verdict and say what it refers to.
title: clone(): shallow vs deep copy, and copy constructors

commonMistakes: Assuming the close exception replaces the body exception.
Printing only getMessage() and never checking getSuppressed().
detailedAnswer: Two exceptions can occur: one from the try body and one from closing a resource. Try-with-resources keeps the body's exception as the primary one and attaches the close exception with addSuppressed, so getSuppressed() returns it instead of it being lost. If the body completes normally and only the close throws, the close exception becomes the primary one. addSuppressed is also available to your own code when combining failures, for example when a cleanup step fails while another exception is already in flight. The point for an interview is the ordering rule: the body wins, the close is suppressed, nothing is silently dropped.
followUps: How do you read the suppressed exceptions from a caught exception?
What happens if the body succeeds but the close throws?
question: What happens to an exception thrown while a try-with-resources resource is closing?
shortAnswer: It is attached to the primary exception as a suppressed exception, retrievable with getSuppressed() — it is not lost, and it never replaces the exception thrown by the try body.
tips: State the ordering rule first: body wins, close is suppressed.
title: Suppressed exceptions in try-with-resources
